Q: How does window.postMessage enable safe cross-origin communication, and what security checks are mandatory?
Why: Strict targetOrigin and event.origin checks prevent cross-origin eavesdropping and malicious message injection.
Risk: Using targetOrigin='*' allows any malicious site embedding your frame to intercept sensitive user tokens and private data.
Trade: Requires maintaining synchronized domain allowlists across environments (development, staging, production).
Try: Send a postMessage with targetOrigin set to wrong domain and observe the browser silently preventing delivery in DevTools.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A fintech payment iframe passes a credit card token back to the parent merchant checkout page. The developer writes window.parent.postMessage({ token }, '*'). An attacker embeds the payment iframe inside attacker.com. When the user clicks pay, postMessage broadcasts to attacker.com, and the attacker's window.onmessage steals the credit card token. Fixing targetOrigin to 'https://merchant.com' causes the browser to block transmission to attacker.com, thwarting the attack.

follow_ups.Q: Can functions or DOM elements be sent across postMessage?
follow_ups.A: No, the Structured Clone Algorithm cannot clone functions, DOM nodes, or symbols; attempting to do so throws a DataCloneError DOMException.

Q: What does the iframe sandbox attribute do, and why is combining allow-scripts with allow-same-origin dangerous?
A:
**Direct answer:** The `sandbox` attribute on an `<iframe>` enables an extra set of strict security restrictions for embedded content. When used with an empty value (`<iframe sandbox src="...">`), it applies maximum lockdown: scripts cannot execute, forms cannot submit, popups cannot open, plugins are disabled, and the embedded frame is treated as having a unique, opaque origin (`null`). Capabilities can be selectively granted using flags (e.g. `allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`).

Crucially, **combining `allow-scripts` with `allow-same-origin` on untrusted content completely destroys the sandbox**: Because `allow-same-origin` grants the iframe its actual origin and `allow-scripts` allows JavaScript execution, a script inside the iframe can simply execute `window.parent.document.querySelector('iframe').removeAttribute('sandbox')`, permanently escaping the sandbox!

```html
<!-- 1. MAXIMUM LOCKDOWN: Scripts, forms, and popups blocked -->
<iframe sandbox src="https://untrusted.com/widget.html"></iframe>

<!-- 2. SAFE SANDBOX FOR THIRD-PARTY SCRIPTS: Scripts allowed, but origin remains 'null' -->
<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" src="https://untrusted.com/widget.html"></iframe>

<!-- 3. CRITICAL VULNERABILITY: Sandboxing completely defeated! -->
<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" src="https://untrusted.com/widget.html"></iframe>
```

**Complexity analysis and mechanics:**
- **Origin coercion:** Without `allow-same-origin`, the iframe's origin is forced to `null`, blocking access to `localStorage`, cookies, and same-origin DOM.
- **Common flags:** `allow-forms` (form submission), `allow-popups` (window.open), `allow-top-navigation` (navigating parent browser tab).

**Algorithmic mechanics and edge cases:**
To safely host user-uploaded untrusted HTML (like previewing markdown or customer emails), serve the content from an entirely isolated secondary domain (e.g., `usercontent.example.com` rather than `app.example.com`) in addition to using `sandbox="allow-scripts"`.
Why: Iframe sandboxing isolates untrusted third-party code from accessing parent cookies, storage, and DOM trees.
Risk: Combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin permits embedded malicious scripts to programmatically remove their own sandbox.
Trade: Strict sandboxing prevents untrusted widgets from accessing cookies or storage, requiring postMessage for state exchange.
Try: Attempt to access window.localStorage inside an iframe with sandbox='allow-scripts' and verify SecurityError is thrown.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A SaaS app allows users to embed custom JavaScript widgets. The app uses sandbox='allow-scripts allow-same-origin'. An attacker crafts a widget containing window.parent.document.cookie. Because allow-same-origin is present, the iframe shares the parent origin, and allow-scripts executes the payload, extracting the parent's session tokens. Removing allow-same-origin forces the iframe into origin null, blocking access to parent DOM and cookies.

follow_ups.Q: What does the allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation sandbox flag enforce?
follow_ups.A: It permits the iframe to navigate the top-level parent window only if the navigation is triggered by a direct user gesture (like a click), blocking automatic programmatic redirects.

Q: How does the BroadcastChannel API coordinate state across multiple browser tabs, and how does it compare to storage events?
Why: BroadcastChannel provides clean, in-memory cross-tab communication without abuse of synchronous localStorage disk writes.
Risk: Forgetting to call channel.close() when components or workers unmount leaks memory and keeps background event listeners active.
Trade: Only functions between windows sharing the exact same origin; cannot communicate across different domains.
Try: Open two tabs of the same app, postMessage on BroadcastChannel in Tab 1, and observe instant console log in Tab 2.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A user opens an online banking app across 3 tabs. In Tab 1, the user clicks 'Log Out'. Tab 1 broadcasts { type: 'LOGOUT' } on authChannel. Tabs 2 and 3 receive the event within 2ms, invalidate their local memory caches, and redirect to the login screen, preventing unauthorized actions on stale open tabs.

follow_ups.Q: Does BroadcastChannel work across different origins (e.g. app.com and api.com)?
follow_ups.A: No, BroadcastChannel strictly enforces the Same-Origin Policy; communication is isolated exclusively to contexts sharing identical protocol, host, and port.

Q: How do you use a SharedWorker to share a single WebSocket connection across multiple open browser tabs?
Why: SharedWorkers eliminate redundant WebSocket connections across tabs, reducing server connection exhaustion by 90%.
Risk: Debugging SharedWorkers requires navigating to chrome://inspect/#workers; standard tab DevTools do not log worker console output.
Trade: Significantly higher architectural complexity; requires MessagePort communication and fallback for unsupported browsers.
Try: Open chrome://inspect/#workers in Google Chrome while running a SharedWorker script and inspect its dedicated console.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An exchange trading platform has 100,000 active users who average 5 open tabs each. Direct WebSockets require 500,000 persistent socket connections on backend servers. Implementing SharedWorker drops total backend connections from 500,000 down to 100,000, slashing infrastructure server costs by 80% while keeping all tabs in perfect sync.

follow_ups.Q: What happens to a SharedWorker when the last open tab using it is closed?
follow_ups.A: The browser automatically closes the worker's ports and terminates the SharedWorker process to free system memory.

Q: Why is window.opener a severe security liability (reverse tabnabbing), and how does rel="noopener noreferrer" prevent it?
A: **Direct answer:** When an HTML link includes `target="_blank"` without protection, the newly opened tab receives a JavaScript reference to the originating window via `window.opener`. This creates a severe security vulnerability known as **Reverse Tabnabbing**: the newly opened external website can execute `window.opener.location = 'https://phishing-site.com'` in the background while the user is looking at the new tab. When the user switches back to their original tab, they see a convincing fake login page asking for their credentials. ```html Visit Partner Visit Partner ``` ```typescript // Programmatic window.open() safety: const newWindow = window.open('https://external.com', '_blank', 'noopener,noreferrer'); // If noopener is omitted: if (newWindow) newWindow.opener = null; // Immediately sever opener reference! ``` **Complexity analysis and mechanics:** - **`rel="noopener"`:** Instructs the browser to set `window.opener` to `null` in the new browsing context and runs the new window in an isolated process thread. - **`rel="noreferrer"`:** Additionally strips the HTTP `Referer` request header, preventing the destination website from learning the URL of the originating page. **Algorithmic mechanics and edge cases:** Modern browsers (Chrome 88+, Firefox 79+, Safari 12.1+) now default `target="_blank"` on `` tags to `rel="noopener"` automatically. However, programmatic `window.open(url, '_blank')` calls still leak `window.opener` unless `'noopener'` is explicitly passed in window features!
Why: Severing window.opener prevents untrusted external links from redirecting the user's active session to phishing pages.
Risk: Calling window.open() programmatically without noopener leaves the parent application vulnerable to reverse tabnabbing.
Trade: Setting window.opener = null prevents legitimate popups (like OAuth dialogs) from signaling back to the parent without postMessage.
Try: Open a target='_blank' link without noopener to a page with window.opener.location='https://example.com' and observe parent redirect.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A developer creates a link to an external blog: <a href="..." target="_blank">. The external blog gets hacked. The hacker's page executes window.opener.location = 'https://fake-login-prompt.com'. The user closes the blog and sees the login prompt on the original tab, enters their password, and gets compromised. Adding rel="noopener noreferrer" sets window.opener to null, preventing the external page from touching the parent tab.

follow_ups.Q: Does modern Chrome default target='_blank' to noopener automatically?
follow_ups.A: Yes, Chrome 88+ defaults anchor tags with target='_blank' to rel='noopener', but programmatic window.open() calls still require explicit noopener.

Q: How do you design a bi-directional RPC message-passing protocol over postMessage with request-response correlation?
Why: UUID correlation transforms asynchronous, decoupled postMessage calls into clean async/await Promise functions.
Risk: Failing to implement timeout cleanup causes pending promise maps to grow unbounded if the target iframe fails to respond.
Trade: Adds wrapper protocol serialization overhead to enable synchronous-feeling request/response communication.
Try: Implement IframeRPCClient and test invoking a mock 'calculateTax' method inside an embedded iframe with async/await.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A parent app embeds a sandboxed checkout iframe and needs to query validateAddress(address). Calling client.call('validateAddress', addr) generates UUID-101, stores the promise in this.pending, and sends postMessage. The iframe verifies the address and replies with { id: 'UUID-101', type: 'RESPONSE', result: { valid: true } }. The parent resolves the promise, allowing the checkout step to proceed with standard async/await syntax.

follow_ups.Q: What open source library popularizes using ES6 Proxies over postMessage for RPC?
follow_ups.A: Comlink (by Google Chrome Labs) uses ES6 Proxies to make objects in Web Workers or iframes feel like local asynchronous JavaScript objects.

Q: How do X-Frame-Options and Content Security Policy frame-ancestors protect applications against Clickjacking attacks?
A:
**Direct answer:** Clickjacking (UI Redressing) is an attack where an attacker embeds a vulnerable target website inside an invisible (`opacity: 0.0001`), framed `<iframe>` placed directly over an enticing visual decoy (e.g. 'Click here to win a prize!'). When the user clicks the decoy, they are unknowingly clicking buttons inside the transparent framed application (e.g., 'Transfer Funds' or 'Delete Account').

Defenses are enforced via HTTP response headers:
1. **`Content Security Policy: frame-ancestors` (Modern Standard):** Dictates which origins are permitted to embed the page in `<frame>`, `<iframe>`, `<object>`, or `<embed>`.
   - `frame-ancestors 'none';` -> Completely prohibits all embedding (most secure).
   - `frame-ancestors 'self';` -> Only permits pages on the exact same origin to embed it.
   - `frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted-partner.com;` -> Explicit allowlist.
2. **`X-Frame-Options` (Legacy Defense):**
   - `X-Frame-Options: DENY` -> Blocks all framing.
   - `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` -> Only same-origin embedding allowed.

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';
X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

**Complexity analysis and mechanics:**
- **Header precedence:** If both are present, modern browsers ignore `X-Frame-Options` in favor of `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors`.
- **Why framebusting JS scripts fail:** Legacy JavaScript framebusting scripts (`if (top !== self) top.location = self.location`) can be defeated by attackers using `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">`, which prevents top-level navigation while permitting scripts to run.

**Algorithmic mechanics and edge cases:**
`X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM` is deprecated and ignored by modern browsers. If you need to allow specific multiple partner origins to embed your application, you must use CSP `frame-ancestors`.
Why: frame-ancestors blocks framing at the browser network layer before malicious UI overlay clicks can be executed.
Risk: Relying on JavaScript framebusting scripts fails because sandboxed iframes can restrict top navigation, neutralizing the script.
Trade: frame-ancestors 'none' prevents legitimate embedding; partners must be explicitly enumerated in the policy.
Try: Configure Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' on an endpoint and attempt to embed it in an iframe in DevTools.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An attacker creates free-movies.com and embeds bank.com/transfer inside an invisible iframe directly over a 'Play Movie' button. A logged-in user clicks 'Play' and unknowingly transfers \$500 to the attacker. When bank.com deploys Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none', the browser refuses to render the iframe inside free-movies.com, displaying a grey frame block and completely defeating the clickjacking exploit.

follow_ups.Q: Why is X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM deprecated in modern web standards?
follow_ups.A: ALLOW-FROM was inconsistently implemented across browsers and only supported a single domain; CSP frame-ancestors supersedes it with full domain list support.

Q: What is WindowProxy in the browser environment, and what properties can be accessed across origins under SOP?
Why: WindowProxy preserves window references across navigations while strictly enforcing cross-origin property access security.
Risk: Attempting to read properties like popup.location.href across origins crashes the script with an unhandled SecurityError.
Trade: Allows basic window orchestration (navigating, closing, messaging) without exposing private DOM, cookies, or URLs.
Try: Open a cross-origin window.open('https://google.com') in the browser console and inspect which properties can be read without errors.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An OAuth login flow opens window.open('https://auth.provider.com'). The parent sets an interval: const timer = setInterval(() => { if (popup.closed) { clearInterval(timer); handleCancel(); } }, 500). Because popup.closed is one of the five permitted cross-origin properties on WindowProxy, the parent reliably detects user cancellation without triggering SecurityError.

follow_ups.Q: Why is writing to window.location.href permitted across origins, but reading it is blocked?
follow_ups.A: Writing allows navigating the window to a new destination; reading it is blocked because the URL may contain sensitive tokens, session IDs, or private path parameters.

Q: How do you safely resize responsive embedded iframes dynamically using ResizeObserver and postMessage?
Why: ResizeObserver paired with postMessage delivers seamless auto-resizing iframe embeds without ugly double scrollbars.
Risk: Failing to round heights or threshold changes can trigger infinite oscillation loops where height changes cause scrollbar toggling.
Trade: Requires deploying cooperative messaging code on both the parent container and child iframe documents.
Try: Observe document.documentElement with ResizeObserver inside an iframe and log heights as dynamic content is appended.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A customer support chat widget lives inside an iframe on an e-commerce store. When collapsed, the widget is 60px high. When the user clicks 'Chat', the widget expands to 450px. ResizeObserver inside the iframe detects the DOM height increase and posts { type: 'IFRAME_RESIZE', height: 450 } to the parent. The parent sets iframe.style.height = '450px' in 1 frame, eliminating scrollbars.

follow_ups.Q: What causes infinite resize loops in auto-resizing iframes?
follow_ups.A: If the child height calculation includes scrollbars that disappear once expanded, the height shrinks, reintroducing scrollbars and looping endlessly.

Q: How does the StorageEvent API detect and synchronize localStorage mutations across different open windows?
Why: StorageEvent enables multi-tab session synchronization and immediate cross-tab logout with zero library dependencies.
Risk: Assuming the storage event fires in the tab that called setItem(); it only fires in other peer tabs.
Trade: localStorage writes are synchronous and block the main thread; BroadcastChannel is preferred for high-frequency messaging.
Try: Open two tabs of the same origin, execute localStorage.setItem('foo', 'bar') in Tab 1, and inspect window.onstorage in Tab 2.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A user opens an e-commerce site in two tabs. In Tab 1, the user adds a jacket to the cart. localStorage.setItem('cart_items', JSON.stringify(cart)) executes. Tab 2 receives the StorageEvent with key='cart_items', parses the new cart JSON, and updates the cart badge icon from '0' to '1' immediately without requiring a page refresh.

follow_ups.Q: Does the storage event fire when sessionStorage is modified?
follow_ups.A: No, sessionStorage is scoped strictly to the current top-level browsing context and tab; it never synchronizes across different tabs.

Q: How do you securely embed and sandbox a third-party checkout widget or authentication modal inside an iframe?
Why: Granular sandbox flags and strict origin filtering isolate payment tokenization from main application vulnerabilities.
Risk: Granting allow-top-navigation permits a compromised widget to redirect the user's browser away to a phishing site.
Trade: Prevents direct DOM interaction, requiring all configuration and token handshakes to travel over postMessage.
Try: Inspect an embedded Stripe Elements iframe in Chrome DevTools to observe its sandbox, permissions, and postMessage architecture.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An e-commerce store needs to achieve PCI-DSS SAQ-A compliance. By rendering credit card inputs inside an iframe hosted by Stripe on js.stripe.com, credit card numbers never touch the merchant's DOM, JavaScript memory, or servers. The iframe collects card details, tokenizes with Stripe, and sends { token: 'tok_123' } to the parent via postMessage.

follow_ups.Q: Why does PCI-DSS compliance favor iframe embedding over direct client-side API requests for credit cards?
follow_ups.A: With iframes, card numbers are entered directly into the payment processor's isolated DOM, keeping the merchant out of PCI scope (SAQ-A vs SAQ A-EP).

Q: What are the capabilities and security constraints of the Cross-Origin Embedder Policy (COEP) and COOP?
A: **Direct answer:** Following the discovery of microarchitectural CPU side-channel vulnerabilities (Spectre and Meltdown), browsers disabled high-resolution timers (`performance.now()` precision was reduced) and restricted `SharedArrayBuffer` because attackers could measure microsecond cache timing differences across origins within the same process. To safely re-enable `SharedArrayBuffer` and multi-threaded WebAssembly, browsers introduced **Cross-Origin Isolation** enforced via two HTTP headers: 1. **`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` (COOP):** Isolates the browsing context group, ensuring other cross-origin windows cannot obtain a reference to your window via `window.opener`. 2. **`Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (COEP):** Guarantees that any cross-origin resource (images, scripts, iframes) embedded in the page must explicitly opt-in via Cross-Origin Resource Policy (`CORP`) or CORS. ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp ``` ```typescript // Once Cross-Origin Isolation is enabled: if (window.crossOriginIsolated) { // SharedArrayBuffer is unlocked! const sharedBuffer = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024); console.log('SharedArrayBuffer enabled for multi-threaded WebAssembly!'); } ``` **Complexity analysis and mechanics:** - **`window.crossOriginIsolated`:** A boolean property reflecting whether both COOP and COEP are active. - **Impact on embeds:** Any external asset (e.g. ``) without `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin` or CORS will be blocked by the browser. **Algorithmic mechanics and edge cases:** To embed third-party iframes without requiring upstream CORP headers, modern browsers support `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless`, which strips cookies and client credentials from cross-origin requests, satisfying COEP without breaking existing assets.
Why: COOP and COEP create process isolation barriers that safely unlock SharedArrayBuffer and high-precision timers.
Risk: Enabling require-corp breaks third-party images, analytics scripts, and iframes that lack explicit CORP headers.
Trade: Unlocks multi-threaded WebAssembly performance at the cost of requiring all third-party embedded assets to configure CORS/CORP.
Try: Check window.crossOriginIsolated in browser console and observe it is false by default on standard web pages.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An in-browser video editor uses WebAssembly FFmpeg to render 4K video clips. Single-threaded WASM is too slow. Multi-threaded WASM requires SharedArrayBuffer. Setting COOP: same-origin and COEP: require-corp isolates the process, setting crossOriginIsolated = true. SharedArrayBuffer unlocks, and video rendering runs 8x faster across 8 Web Worker CPU threads.

follow_ups.Q: What does COEP: credentialless do as an alternative to require-corp?
follow_ups.A: credentialless loads cross-origin subresources without cookies or authentication headers, allowing them to load without requiring explicit CORP headers.

Q: How do MessageChannel and MessagePort provide private point-to-point communication channels between frames?
Why: MessageChannel creates private point-to-point communication tunnels that third-party scripts on the global window cannot spy on.
Risk: Failing to call port.start() when using addEventListener causes messages to remain permanently queued and unhandled.
Trade: Requires an initial postMessage handshake to transfer the port before point-to-point messaging can begin.
Try: Create a MessageChannel, transfer port2 to a Web Worker, and communicate over port1 without global worker onmessage handlers.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A dashboard hosts two third-party iframes: StockChart and TradeExecution. StockChart needs to stream live tick data directly to TradeExecution. Instead of routing 1,000 messages/sec through the parent window, the parent creates a MessageChannel, passes port1 to StockChart and port2 to TradeExecution. The two iframes stream directly between each other, completely bypassing the parent.

follow_ups.Q: What is the difference between port.onmessage and port.addEventListener('message')?
follow_ups.A: Setting port.onmessage automatically calls port.start() under the hood, whereas addEventListener requires manual port.start() to begin queue processing.

Q: How do you implement cross-tab leader election to ensure only one tab performs background synchronization?
Why: Web Locks API guarantees atomic, crash-resilient leader election across tabs without clock skew or heartbeat polling.
Risk: Resolving the lock promise prematurely releases the lock, allowing another tab to claim leadership concurrently.
Trade: Requires browser support for Web Locks API (supported in all modern browsers since Chrome 69, Safari 15.4, Firefox 96).
Try: Open two tabs using Web Locks leader election, close the active leader tab, and watch the second tab claim leadership instantly.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An application synchronizes IndexedDB with a backend server every 10 seconds. A user opens 8 tabs. Without leader election, all 8 tabs poll the server every 10 seconds (48 requests/min). With TabLeaderElection via Web Locks, Tab 1 acquires the lock and polls the server, sharing results to Tabs 2-8 via BroadcastChannel (6 requests/min). When Tab 1 is closed, Tab 2 claims the lock in 5ms and resumes polling.

follow_ups.Q: What happens if a tab holding a Web Lock crashes or is terminated by the OS?
follow_ups.A: The browser process detects context termination and automatically releases all held locks, instantly granting them to the next waiting tab.

Q: How do iframe credentialless and permission policy attributes restrict embedded frame capabilities?
A:
**Direct answer:** Modern web security enforces least privilege through two granular controls:
1. **`credentialless` attribute:** Loads the `<iframe>` in a new, ephemeral context where network requests omit all ambient credentials (cookies, client certificates, HTTP authentication). This allows embedding cross-origin content within `COEP: require-corp` documents without requiring the embedded origin to configure complex CORS headers.
2. **`allow` (Permissions Policy):** Explicitly defines which browser hardware and sensitive web APIs the embedded iframe is allowed to access (e.g. `camera`, `microphone`, `geolocation`, `payment`, `fullscreen`, `display-capture`). By default, powerful APIs are disabled unless explicitly delegated via `allow`.

```html
<!-- Secure Embedded Video Frame with Least Privilege API Access -->
<iframe
    src="https://videos.partner.com/player/42"
    credentialless
    allow="fullscreen; autoplay; encrypted-media 'src'"
    sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"
    title="Video Player">
</iframe>
```

**Complexity analysis and mechanics:**
- **Permission inheritance:** By default, if the parent page lacks a permission (e.g. user denied geolocation), an iframe cannot access it even if listed in `allow`.
- **Explicit origin scoping:** `allow="camera 'src'"` restricts camera access specifically to the iframe's `src` origin, preventing third-party redirects inside the frame from stealing camera privileges.

**Algorithmic mechanics and edge cases:**
If an iframe attempts to invoke `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia()` without `allow="camera; microphone"`, the browser immediately rejects the promise with a `NotAllowedError` DOMException without prompting the user.
Why: Permissions Policy guarantees embedded widgets cannot secretly access user cameras, microphones, or geolocation sensors.
Risk: Omitting explicit allow attributes or granting allow='*' gives embedded third-party scripts unrestricted hardware access.
Trade: Requires auditing all third-party widget requirements and specifying explicit capability lists on iframe tags.
Try: Attempt to call navigator.geolocation in an iframe without allow='geolocation' and verify NotAllowedError is returned.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: An application embeds an advertising widget. The ad script attempts to silently activate the laptop microphone to record ambient audio for ad targeting. Because the iframe tag specifies allow="fullscreen" and omits microphone, the browser blocks the microphone API call at the hardware layer with zero user prompt.

follow_ups.Q: What is the difference between allow='geolocation *' and allow='geolocation src'?
follow_ups.A: allow='geolocation *' allows any nested document or redirect inside the iframe to use geolocation; 'src' restricts it strictly to the iframe's initial src origin.

Q: How do popups, modal windows, and parent windows securely synchronize OAuth authentication redirects?
Why: Popup OAuth synchronization preserves the parent single-page application's memory and state during authentication.
Risk: Omitting the popup.closed check leaves the parent promise permanently pending if the user closes the popup window manually.
Trade: Popup windows are blocked by mobile Safari and aggressive ad blockers, requiring full-page redirect fallbacks.
Try: Click an OAuth popup button, close the popup without logging in, and verify that the parent catches 'User cancelled login popup'.
worked_case: Walkthrough scenario: A user working on an unsaved 1,000-word blog post needs to re-authenticate with Google. A full-page redirect would blow away the unsaved post. The app opens loginWithOAuth(). The user signs in via the popup. The popup posts the authorization code back to the parent and closes. The parent exchanges the code for a token and saves the post with zero data loss.

follow_ups.Q: Why must popup windows be triggered by a direct user click event?
follow_ups.A: Browsers enforce popup blocker heuristics that automatically block window.open() calls unless initiated by a direct user gesture (like a button click).
